choices.text: The total water a city uses in one year

choices.text: The average water each resident of a city uses in one year

questions.hint: Capita comes from the Latin word for 'heads'. Which choice divides by the number of heads?

questions.units: cubic meters per person per year
questions.conditions: Assume the yearly renewable supply stays the same and all of it is counted as available.
questions.limitations: Real supplies vary from year to year and place to place, and not all renewable water can be captured for use.

questions.workedSolution: Water per person = total supply ÷ number of people = 8,000,000,000 m³ ÷ 2,000,000 people = 4,000 m³ per person per year. Before the growth it was 8,000,000,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = 8,000 m³ per person, so doubling the population halved each person's share.

questions.prompt: Match each case from the lesson to the kind of ecosystem disruption it shows.
questions.accessiblePrompt: Match each case from the lesson to the kind of ecosystem disruption it shows. left.rationale: Taking fish faster than populations can rebuild is over-exploitation.

left.text: Plastic bags and bottles build up in the ocean, where sea turtles swallow them
left.rationale: Adding harmful material to an ecosystem is pollution.

left.text: A virus carried by fruit bats starts infecting pig farmers
left.rationale: A disease newly reaching people through new contact with wildlife is an emerging disease.

left.text: Tropical forest is cut down to plant rows of coffee
left.rationale: Destroying a natural habitat so it no longer works as a forest is habitat degradation.

left.text: Carp from another continent spread through rivers toward the Great Lakes

questions.prompt: Which of these fit the lesson's definition of an invasive species? Select all that apply.
questions.accessiblePrompt: Which of these fit the lesson's definition of an invasive species? Select all that apply. The choices are: a fish people brought from another continent that eats the plankton native fish need and keeps spreading; a water plant people carried in from overseas that spreads quickly and clogs boat channels and fish habitat; a vegetable people brought from another continent that grows in gardens but does not spread or cause harm; and a native songbird that has always lived there, whose numbers rise after several mild winters.

choices.text: A fish people brought from another continent that eats the plankton native fish need and keeps spreading
choices.rationale: Correct: people brought it, and it harms native fish by taking their food.

choices.text: A water plant people carried in from overseas that spreads quickly and clogs boat channels and fish habitat
choices.rationale: Correct: people introduced it, and it causes both ecological and economic harm.

choices.text: A vegetable people brought from another continent that grows in gardens but does not spread or cause harm
choices.rationale: People brought it, but without harm it does not meet the definition of invasive.

choices.text: A native songbird that has always lived there, whose numbers rise after several mild winters

questions.explanation: An invasive species needs two things: people brought it to a place where it does not naturally live, and it causes ecological or economic harm there. questions.misconception: Any species from somewhere else, or any population that grows fast, is invasive.
questions.hint: Check two things for each choice: did people bring it from elsewhere, and does it cause harm?

questions.prompt: Put the steps of the Lake Malawi chain in order, from the first cause to the final effect on people.
questions.accessiblePrompt: Put the steps of the Lake Malawi chain in order, from the first cause to the final effect on people. The steps are: snail populations grow; many more people live near the lake and fish it heavily; more people who wade in the lake become infected with bilharzia; snail-eating fish become much less common; and more parasitic worms develop in the growing snail populations.
questions.conditions: Follow the chain as the lesson describes it, with no other changes in the lake.
questions.limitations: Real lakes have many more species and links than this simple chain.

items.text: Snail populations grow
items.rationale: With fewer predators eating them, snails survive and reproduce in larger numbers.

items.text: Many more people live near the lake and fish it heavily
items.rationale: The human population boom is the first cause in the lesson's chain.

items.text: More people who wade in the lake become infected with bilharzia
items.rationale: The parasites reach people last, as they wade in the water.

items.text: Snail-eating fish become much less common
items.rationale: Heavy fishing removes the snail-eating fish, so this comes right after the fishing increases.

items.text: More parasitic worms develop in the growing snail populations
items.rationale: The worms live in snails for part of their life, so more snails means more worms.

questions.explanation: Heavy fishing removed many of the fish that eat snails, so snails multiplied. Snails host parasitic worms for part of the worms' life, so more snails meant more worms, and more people wading in the water caught bilharzia. questions.misconception: Removing fish only affects the fish; it can't change other species or people's health.
questions.hint: Start with the human change, then follow who eats whom.

evidence.supports: As humans removed more fish, their prey, freshwater snails, increased; snails carry parasitic worms transmitted to people wading in the water, so bilharzia increased.

questions.conditions: Follow the chain as described for Long Island Sound, starting with the pollution.

items.text: Algae grow quickly in the nitrogen-rich water
items.rationale: Nitrogen is a nutrient, so algae grow fast once it enters the water.

items.text: Lobsters, fish and oysters struggle to get enough oxygen and their numbers drop
items.rationale: Animals suffer last, once the oxygen has been used up.

items.text: Sewage treatment plants release water carrying extra nitrogen

items.text: Bacteria breaking down the dead algae use up dissolved oxygen

items.text: Large amounts of algae die and sink
items.rationale: A huge bloom of algae eventually dies and settles toward the bottom.

questions.explanation: Extra nitrogen acts like fertilizer for algae, so they grow fast. When the algae die and sink, bacteria decompose them and use up oxygen in the water, especially near the bottom. Animals that need dissolved oxygen, such as lobsters, fish and oysters, then decline.
questions.misconception: Nitrogen harms sea animals directly, like a poison, rather than through a chain of effects.
questions.hint: Nitrogen feeds producers. Ask what happens when a huge crop of producers dies.

evidence.locator: Section 8, Comparing Ecosystem Conditions to the Model
evidence.supports: Sewage treatment plants are the biggest nitrogen source; high nitrogen increases algae growth; decomposition of algae lowers oxygen; low oxygen reduces lobsters, fish and oysters.

evidence.title: Hypoxia (ecosystem target indicator)
evidence.supports: Bacterial respiration while decomposing sunken algae is the largest cause of low oxygen in the Sound's bottom water; after nitrogen cuts at wastewater plants, the hypoxic area fell from a 1987-1999 average of 208 square miles to a 2021-2025 average of 83 square miles, about a 60 percent reduction.

evidence.title: What is a dead zone?
evidence.supports: Excess nutrients from runoff and wastewater feed algae overgrowth; when the algae die and decompose, the decomposition consumes oxygen.

questions.prompt: The graph shows a computer-model prediction of sea-level change, with a shaded band around the main line. Why does the band get wider toward 2100?
questions.accessiblePrompt: A graph shows a computer-model prediction of sea-level change from 1950 to about 2095. The main line rises slowly at first and then faster and faster. A shaded band around the line is very narrow up to about 2030, then widens: around 2095 it spans from about 88 to about 137 centimeters, around a middle value of about 112 centimeters. Why does the band get wider toward 2100?

diagram.caption: One model's predicted sea-level change, with a shaded range (values read from the textbook graph)
diagram.alt: Line graph of predicted sea-level change in centimeters from 1950 to about 2095. The middle line starts near minus 8 centimeters in 1950, passes 0 around 1980, about 22 in 2030, about 43 in 2050, about 70 in 2070 and about 112 around 2095, rising faster and faster. The upper and lower estimates are almost the same as the middle line until about 2030, then spread apart: about 38 to 48 centimeters in 2050, 60 to 80 in 2070, and 88 to 137 around 2095.

questions.limitations: Numbers come from the textbook's graph and are dated; current NOAA and IPCC projections differ. Only the widening of the range is being tested.

choices.text: Predictions further ahead are less certain; they depend on future emissions and ice melt
choices.rationale: Correct: the range grows because the far future depends on choices and processes not yet known.

choices.text: Scientists have been measuring sea level less carefully in recent years than back in the 1950s
choices.rationale: The band is narrow for past years and widens only for the future, so it is not about old measurements.

choices.text: The band shows daily tides, which are expected to get much bigger in the future
choices.rationale: The band shows a range of predictions for average sea level, not the daily rise and fall of tides.

choices.text: The band shows that the sea will rise for a while and then fall again before 2100
choices.rationale: Every part of the band keeps rising; it shows uncertainty about how much, not a fall.

questions.explanation: The band shows the range of likely outcomes. Predictions further in the future are less certain, because sea-level rise depends on how much greenhouse gas people emit and on how fast ice sheets melt. Planners use the whole range, not one exact number.
questions.misconception: A model prediction should be one exact number, so a range means the scientists know nothing.
questions.hint: Think about which is harder to predict: next decade or the end of the century.

questions.prompt: An ecosystem service is a benefit that a healthy ecosystem gives people. Which of these is an ecosystem service?
questions.accessiblePrompt: An ecosystem service is a benefit that a healthy ecosystem gives people. Which of these is an ecosystem service? The choices are: a coastal marsh soaking up storm floodwater before it reaches nearby homes; a city building a concrete seawall to hold back storm waves; a water-treatment plant using filters and chemicals to clean a city's drinking water; and volunteers picking up plastic trash along a beach.

choices.text: A coastal marsh soaking up storm floodwater before it reaches nearby homes
choices.rationale: Correct: the marsh itself provides the benefit, so this is a service from a healthy ecosystem.

choices.text: A city building a concrete seawall to hold back storm waves
choices.rationale: A seawall can protect people, but people built it; an ecosystem service is a benefit that nature provides.

choices.text: A water-treatment plant using filters and chemicals to clean a city's drinking water
choices.rationale: This is an engineered service; healthy wetlands clean water naturally, but a treatment plant is a human-built system.

choices.text: Volunteers picking up plastic trash along a beach
choices.rationale: This helps an ecosystem, which is the opposite direction: an ecosystem service is a benefit flowing from nature to people.

questions.explanation: Ecosystem services flow from nature to people: wetlands store floodwater and improve water quality, and ecosystems supply food and medicines. Seawalls and treatment plants are human-built ways to get similar benefits, often at a high cost. A beach cleanup is people helping an ecosystem, which is the reverse.
questions.misconception: An ecosystem service is something people do for an ecosystem, or any service that protects people.
questions.hint: Ask who or what is providing the benefit: nature, or something people built or did?

questions.prompt: Asian carp populations keep growing in U.S. rivers. Which facts from the lesson help explain why? Select all that apply.

The choices are: they have few predators in their new home; they eat huge amounts of plankton, a food found throughout the rivers; they are a native species that has always lived in these rivers; and they feed on weeds that native fish ignore, so they face no competition.

choices.text: They have few predators in their new home
choices.rationale: Correct: with little to eat them, more carp survive to reproduce each year.

choices.text: They eat huge amounts of plankton, a food found throughout the rivers
choices.rationale: Correct: a large, widespread food supply lets their numbers climb, and it leaves less for native fish.

choices.text: They are a native species that has always lived in these rivers
choices.rationale: People brought them from Eurasia, so they are not native; that is part of what makes them invasive.

choices.text: They feed on weeds that native fish ignore, so they face no competition
choices.rationale: The lesson says they eat plankton that native fish also need, so they do compete, and native fish lose out.

questions.explanation: In their new home, Asian carp have few predators and plenty of plankton to eat, so more of them survive and reproduce. questions.hint: Think about what usually keeps a population in check: what eats it, and how much food it can find.

questions.limitations: 'Asian carp' is a group of several species with somewhat different diets, and federal agencies now call them invasive carp.
